title: Generic Counter
story: You're building an analytics dashboard — counting website visits, tracking error messages, logging user actions. You could write three separate counters... or you could write ONE generic counter that counts ANY type of item.
why: Generic types wrapping Vec let you build reusable data structures — a counter that tracks items of any type, with add, count, clear, and list operations that work universally.
analogy: A Counter[T] is like a tally sheet — you can tally apples sold, customers served, or errors logged. The sheet works the same way regardless of what you're counting. One sheet design, infinite counting possibilities.
try_it: Add a `Counter.most_common[T](self) -> Option[T]` method that returns the item that appears most frequently. Use a Map[T, Int] internally to count frequencies, then scan to find the max. Test with a Counter[Str] tracking words. Then add a `Counter.sum[T](self) -> Option[T]` that only works for... wait, how do you add generic T values? (Another L6 interface topic!)
tips: Type parameter `[T]` propagates: if the type has `[T]`, every method that uses it also needs `[T]`
Constructors conventionally return the type: `fn Counter.new[T]() -> Counter[T]` is a factory pattern
Generic types can be used as fields: `items: Vec[T]` works because Vec itself is generic
common_mistakes: Forgetting `[T]` on every method — `fn Counter.count(self)` is wrong; must be `fn Counter.count[T](self)`
Using `var` when `let` would work — Counter methods that only read should use `let` ownership, not `var`
Returning `self.items` directly — this would move the Vec out; use a while loop to copy items instead
